 Almost no sci-fi book, movie, or show was intentionally written to be an etched-in-stone prophecy. Yet, some additions to the sci-fi genre project a potential future in such an incredible way that they almost come off as documentaries in hindsight. Movies like The Matrix and shows like Black Mirror are often cited as examples of how sci-fi can blur the lines between speculative fiction and reality.

 However, there is one Jonathan Nolan series, titled Person of Interest , that seems far more grounded in reality than even some of the best sci-fi shows and movies. It premiered almost 15 years ago, walking through some intriguing " projections " surrounding the state of surveillance, artificial intelligence, corporate control, and privacy in the future.
 A decade and a half later, Person of Interest almost feels prophetic. Unlike Black Mirror and The Matrix , Person of Interest 's portrayal of a realistic future is not merely confined to metaphors. The show may be relatively obscure, but it perfectly captures how " Life imitates art far more than art imitates life ."
 Person Of Interest Is One Of The Most Realistic Sci-Fi Shows
 Michael Emerson as Harold Finch holding a pair of binoculars in Person of Interest Image via MovieStillsDB 
 Person of Interest 's premise centers on an AI called " The Machine " developed by Harold Finch to help the government foresee terrorist attacks. Like modern-day algorithms, " The Machine " in Person of Interest was developed by tapping into The Feed. Data from CCTV footage, internet searches, and ATMs from across the globe is stitched together to build the AI.
 While there is no centralized program like " The Machine " in the real world, every digital activity creates a solid footprint. The same footprint is then fed into larger systems to manipulate everything from consumer buying decisions to their voting choices.
 Instead of portraying " The Machine " as a one-dimensional AI villain, Person of Interest also brilliantly captures how its creator attempts to stop it from evolving. He not only erases its memory every night but also plays chess with it to help it understand morality and the importance of human life. 
 With this, the show seems to clearly parallel the growing concerns surrounding moral alignments of superintelligence systems and how connecting them to the open internet can help them evolve beyond control. The sci-fi series even introduces a rival AI named Samaritan. Unlike " The Machine, " Samaritan in Person in Interest has no moral guardrails.
 This mirrors the ultimate danger humanity can eventually face in the real world after blindly trusting algorithms and putting all faith in systems that are getting increasingly complex. 
 Person Of Interest Deserves More Attention For Being Incredibly Prophetic
 Reese (Jim Caviezel) and Finch (Michael Emerson) look at a computer in Person of Interest. MovieStills DB 
 The more Person of Interest progresses, the more it becomes a cautionary tale about how human autonomy is slowly stripped when surveillance is normalized and machines control the decisions of the masses. It even introduces real cybersecurity concepts while walking through a gritty procedural drama with relatable characters.
 In one of its most prophetic story developments, Person of Interest even seemingly " predicted " Edward Snowden's revelations surrounding the extent of government surveillance. Not a lot of sci-fi shows have managed to be as spot-on about the future as Person of Interest . While most shows drop narrative resolutions, some of Person of Interest 's best payoffs have been in the real world. 
 Surprisingly, despite being a realistic sci-fi masterpiece, it never achieved mainstream success. Hopefully, the show will garner a bigger audience in the near future and get the attention it has always deserved.

 Person of Interest: Released in 2011, Person of Interest follows former CIA operative John Reese, believed to be dead, as he partners with reclusive billionaire Harold Finch. Together, they use advanced surveillance technology to preemptively address violent crimes in New York City, working outside traditional legal frameworks to deliver justice.
